title: Practitioner Exam
description: 40 questions covering all five modules, drawn from a pool of 50. Pass mark is 80%. This is an open-book exam — take your time, browse any module to refresh your memory, or ask the AI assistant for help. Your answers are saved as you go, so leaving the page to look something up is fine. Explanations show after submission so you can learn from any answers you missed.

questions.scenario: A Transformation executes successfully on one developer's machine but fails with a file-not-found error when run by a colleague, despite using the same transformation file (.ktr) and accessing the same shared source files.
questions.prompt: What is the most probable reason for this discrepancy?
options: A configured file path relies on a variable defined in a `.properties` file, and this variable has a different value or is not defined on the colleague's machine.
The colleague is using a different version of Spoon, causing it to interpret step settings, including file paths, incorrectly.
The source file requires re-importation into Spoon on each machine before it can be accessed by the transformation.
The transformation file (.ktr) contains absolute file paths, making it non-portable and restricted to the environment where it was originally created.
questions.explanation: 'A configured file path relies on a variable defined in the `kettle.properties` file, and this variable has a different value or is not defined on the colleague's machine.' — Correct: The `kettle.properties` file is environment-specific. Variables defined there will resolve differently (or not at all) on different machines. 'The colleague is using a different version of Spoon, causing it to interpret step settings, including file paths, incorrectly.' — Incorrect: While version mismatches can cause issues, they typically don't manifest as a simple file-not-found error. Different versions would likely cause a different type of error. 'The source file requires re-importation into Spoon on each machine before it can be accessed by the transformation.' — Incorrect: PDI reads files directly based on their path; re-importing is not required, and has no effect on execution. 'The transformation file (.ktr) contains absolute file paths, making it non-portable and restricted to the environment where it was originally created.' — Incorrect: Using absolute paths would indeed cause portability issues, but is a poor practice and not the most *probable* cause given the scenario.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Getting Started — Configuring PDI

questions.scenario: A development team needs to define a standard database hostname and an input folder path for all Pentaho Data Integration (PDI) transformations and jobs running on each server. They want to avoid hard-coding these values directly into each transformation or job.
questions.prompt: Which configuration file should be used to store these values so they can be referenced across all PDI jobs and transformations on a given machine?
options: kettle.properties
repositories.xml
.spoonrc
shared.xml
questions.explanation: 'kettle.properties' — Correct: This file is loaded by PDI at startup and allows defining variables that can be used throughout transformations and jobs using the `${variable_name}` syntax. 'repositories.xml' — Incorrect: This file defines connections to data repositories, not general configuration variables. 'shared.xml' — Incorrect: This file is used for defining and managing shared objects, such as database connections, for reuse, but does not store general configuration values like hostnames or folder paths.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Getting Started — Kettle Variables

questions.scenario: A data integration developer is configuring a 'Text file input' step in Pentaho Data Integration (PDI). The desired input file path should be dynamically determined at runtime using a Kettle variable named INPUT_PATH, rather than being hardcoded within the step configuration.
questions.prompt: Which expression should be used in the 'Filename' field of the Text file input step to reference the value of the INPUT_PATH variable?
options: $INPUT_PATH$
%INPUT_PATH%
@INPUT_PATH
${INPUT_PATH}
questions.explanation: '${INPUT_PATH}' — Correct: This is the correct syntax for referencing Kettle variables within PDI steps. The `${}` notation tells PDI to resolve the variable at runtime. '%INPUT_PATH%' — Incorrect: This syntax is commonly used for variable expansion in Windows command-line environments, but it is not recognized by PDI. '@INPUT_PATH' — Incorrect: This syntax is used for parameter referencing in some SQL dialects, but it is not valid for resolving Kettle variables within PDI.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Getting Started — Kettle Variables

questions.scenario: A Pentaho Data Integration developer modifies the `kettle.properties` file on their Windows workstation to adjust a system-level setting. After restarting Spoon, the change is not reflected in the application's behavior, leading them to suspect an issue with the configuration file location.
questions.prompt: By default, where does Pentaho Data Integration (PDI) locate the `kettle.properties` file on a Windows system?
options: %USERPROFILE%\.kettle\kettle.properties
%APPDATA%\Pentaho\kettle.properties
C:\Pentaho\design-tools\data-integration\kettle.properties
C:\ProgramData\Pentaho\kettle.properties
questions.explanation: '%USERPROFILE%\.kettle\kettle.properties' — Correct: PDI prioritizes the `kettle.properties` file located in the user’s home directory, specifically within the `.kettle` folder. This allows for user-specific configurations. '%APPDATA%\Pentaho\kettle.properties' — Incorrect: While `%APPDATA%` is a standard per-user application data directory, PDI does not use it to locate `kettle.properties` by default. 'C:\Pentaho\design-tools\data-integration\kettle.properties' — Incorrect: This path points to the PDI installation directory, which contains the application files but not user-specific configuration files. 'C:\ProgramData\Pentaho\kettle.properties' — Incorrect: The `ProgramData` folder is for system-wide, machine-level data and is not the default location for user-specific PDI configurations.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Getting Started — Kettle Variables

questions.scenario: A data engineer opens Pentaho Spoon to begin designing a new transformation. Instead of the graphical design canvas, the application displays a calendar and scheduling interface.
questions.prompt: Which perspective must be selected to access the transformation design canvas?
options: Data Modeling
Scheduling
Visualization
Data Integration
questions.explanation: 'Data Integration' — Correct: This perspective provides the graphical canvas for designing and building PDI transformations and jobs. 'Data Modeling' — Incorrect: This perspective is used for creating analytical models, not for building data integration workflows. 'Scheduling' — Incorrect: This perspective is used for defining and monitoring the execution of transformations and jobs, not designing them. 'Visualization' — Incorrect: This perspective focuses on data exploration and graphical representation, not transformation design.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Getting Started — Configuring PDI

questions.scenario: A Pentaho Data Integration (PDI) transformation is designed to process customer data from a text file. A transformation designer has connected a 'Text file input' step directly to a 'Filter rows' step using a hop.
questions.prompt: What is the primary function of the hop between the 'Text file input' step and the 'Filter rows' step when the transformation executes?
options: The hop carries rows read from the text file to the filter for evaluation.
The hop re-reads the text file if the filter encounters an error.
The hop schedules the filter step to run after the text file input is complete.
The hop copies configuration parameters from the input step to the filter step.
questions.explanation: 'The hop carries rows read from the text file to the filter for evaluation.' — Correct: A hop defines the flow of data (rows) between steps in a transformation. 'The hop re-reads the text file if the filter encounters an error.' — Incorrect: Hops are for data flow, not error handling or retries, which are typically managed through job entries or step-level error handling. 'The hop schedules the filter step to run after the text file input is complete.' — Incorrect: Transformation steps execute concurrently or sequentially based on hop connections, not scheduling. 'The hop copies configuration parameters from the input step to the filter step.' — Incorrect: While steps can share variables, a hop itself does not copy configuration settings; these are defined within each step.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Concepts & Terminology — Hello World

questions.scenario: A data integration specialist is building a transformation with multiple steps. They need to verify the data flowing into step four, without fully executing the entire transformation and writing output files.
questions.prompt: What primary function does the Preview feature provide that a standard Run execution does not?
options: Executes transformation steps up to a specified step and displays the resulting data rows.
Executes the entire transformation, but suppresses the writing of output data to files.
Performs a faster execution of the transformation by skipping data validation checks.
Generates a sample output based on the transformation’s logic, without actually processing data.
questions.explanation: 'Executes transformation steps up to a specified step and displays the resulting data rows' — Correct: This accurately describes the core functionality of the Preview feature, allowing focused debugging. 'Executes the entire transformation, but suppresses the writing of output data to files' — Incorrect: Preview stops execution at the specified step; it does not complete the entire transformation. 'Performs a faster execution of the transformation by skipping data validation checks' — Incorrect: While Preview might be quicker due to early termination, it does not bypass validation. 'Generates a sample output based on the transformation’s logic, without actually processing data' — Incorrect: Preview relies on actual data processing, not a simulated output.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Concepts & Terminology — Hello World

questions.scenario: A data integration developer is troubleshooting a transformation that processes sensitive customer data. They need to examine the data flowing through each step to identify the source of a data quality issue.
questions.prompt: Which logging level will capture the actual data values for each row as the transformation executes?
options: Detailed
Basic
Row Level
Debug
questions.explanation: 'Row Level' — Correct: This logging level provides the most granular output, including the contents of each row as it passes through each step of the transformation. 'Detailed' — Incorrect: Detailed logging adds information about the execution of each step, such as timings and resource usage, but does not include the actual row data. 'Basic' — Incorrect: Basic logging only records the start and end of the transformation and the total number of rows processed by each step. 'Debug' — Incorrect: Debug logging captures internal diagnostic messages intended for developers but does not display the row-level data.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Concepts & Terminology — Logging

questions.scenario: A transformation reads data from a source and sends it to two downstream steps: one writes the data to a text file, and the other inserts it into a database table. When defining the second hop from the initial step, you selected the 'Copy' option in the dialog box.
questions.prompt: How does the 'Copy' hop type determine the flow of data to the connected steps?
options: Each row of data is sent to both the file writing step and the database table step.
Data is sent alternately to the file writing step, then the database table step, repeating until all rows are processed.
The transformation will fail, as a step can only have one output hop.
Only the first step connected to the source step will receive any data.
questions.explanation: 'Each row of data is sent to both the file writing step and the database table step.' — Correct: The 'Copy' hop type duplicates the data stream, sending every row to all connected steps. 'Data is sent alternately to the file writing step, then the database table step, repeating until all rows are processed.' — Incorrect: This describes the behavior of the 'Distribute' hop type, not 'Copy'. 'The transformation will fail, as a step can only have one output hop.' — Incorrect: A step in a Pentaho Data Integration transformation can have multiple output hops. 'Only the first step connected to the source step will receive any data.' — Incorrect: When using 'Copy', all connected steps receive data, not just the first one.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Concepts & Terminology

questions.scenario: A data integration specialist is building a Transformation to process customer records. The specialist needs detailed logging of specific field values as the data flows through the transformation, to help with debugging and monitoring data quality.
questions.prompt: Which Transformation step is designed to write custom messages, including field values, to the execution log for each processed row?
options: Set variables, with a message field
Text file output, configured to append to a log file
Write to log
Abort, configured to include a diagnostic message
questions.explanation: 'Write to log' — Correct: This step specifically allows for writing custom messages, including field values, to the execution log for each row processed. 'Set variables, with a message field' — Incorrect: While this step can set variables with text, it does not directly write to the execution log on a per-row basis. 'Text file output, configured to append to a log file' — Incorrect: This step writes data to a separate text file, not the execution log within Pentaho. 'Abort, configured to include a diagnostic message' — Incorrect: Abort stops the transformation and writes a message, but it does not provide per-row logging of field values.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Concepts & Terminology — Logging

questions.scenario: A data integration process uses a Table output step configured to handle errors. When an attempt to insert a row into the target database fails, the row is routed to an error handling hop, appending data to a designated text file for review.
questions.prompt: What information is included in each row written to the error file?
options: The complete row data, along with fields containing the error description, error codes, and the specific fields that caused the error.
Only the error message, presented as a single field within the error file row.
The Java exception stack trace generated when the insertion attempt failed.
Only the row's key fields and an error flag.
questions.explanation: 'The complete row data, along with fields containing the error description, error codes, and the specific fields that caused the error.' — Correct: The Table output error handling mechanism preserves the entire row for investigation, and appends details on the error itself. 'Only the error message, presented as a single field within the error file row.' — Incorrect: This doesn't provide enough context for debugging or reprocessing the failed row. The complete row is required. 'The Java exception stack trace generated when the insertion attempt failed.' — Incorrect: While the stack trace might be logged elsewhere, it is not included directly in the error file row. The primary goal of the error file is to capture the problematic data, not debugging information.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Concepts & Terminology — Error Handling

questions.scenario: A nightly load can meet two kinds of trouble: a handful of rows failing validation, and the source file arriving with zero rows when a thousand were expected.
questions.prompt: Which of the two should the Abort step handle?
options: The failing rows, as Abort is how rows are diverted
Neither, as Abort stops only the step it sits in
The empty file, since loading it would wipe good data
Both, as Abort is how any error should be handled
questions.explanation: An empty file is a bad run rather than a bad row: loading it would quietly replace yesterday's data with nothing, so stopping everything is right. Failing rows are a routing decision; send them down a reject branch and the good rows still load. Aborting on every error is far too blunt for bad rows. Abort stops the whole transformation, not just its own step.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Concepts & Terminology — Error Handling

questions.scenario: A Calculator step in the middle of your transformation produces odd totals. You want to see the rows it outputs without running the transformation to the end.
questions.prompt: How do you do that in Spoon?
options: Open the Calculator in a separate workspace
Run the transformation and read the log
Add a text file output and run to the end
Select the Calculator step and preview it
questions.explanation: Previewing the Calculator runs only the steps it needs and shows the rows it outputs, without running to the end. Running and reading the log runs everything and shows no rows unless the log level is raised. Adding a file output still runs to the end and writes a file. A separate workspace does not execute the step at all.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Concepts & Terminology — Hello World

questions.scenario: You are loading a CSV whose first line holds column names rather than data, using a Text file input step.
questions.prompt: How do you make the step treat that first line as a header?
options: Enable Lazy conversion on the Content tab
Run Get Fields with the first row selected
Drop the first row with Filter rows
Tick Header on the Content tab
questions.explanation: Ticking Header on the Content tab, with one header line, tells the step to read the first line as field names. A Filter rows step could discard the line, but only after it was read as data with every field forced to string. Lazy conversion delays type conversion for speed and has nothing to do with headers. Get Fields reads the header once the setting is on; it does not set it.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Text File Input

questions.scenario: An orders.json document holds an array under orders, and each order has a nested customer object with an email field. You are configuring a JSON input step to read one row per order.
questions.prompt: Which expression reads each order's customer email?
options: orders.customer.email
/orders/order/customer/email
$.orders[*].customer.email
$.customer.email[*]
questions.explanation: $.orders[*].customer.email is JSONPath: every element of the orders array, then its customer object, then email. /orders/order/customer/email is XPath, which the XML steps use. orders.customer.email has no root and no array step, so it does not select each order. $.customer.email[*] looks for a customer object at the top level, which does not exist.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Read JSON

questions.scenario: A supplier sends invoices as XML: an <invoices> root holding <invoice> elements, each with an <amount> child. You configure Get data from XML to read one row per invoice.
questions.prompt: What should the step use as its loop path?
options: $.invoices.invoice[*]
/invoices/invoice
//amount
invoices > invoice
questions.explanation: The loop path is an XPath naming the repeating element, /invoices/invoice, and each field such as amount is then read relative to it. $.invoices.invoice[*] is JSONPath, for JSON input. invoices > invoice is a CSS selector, which the step does not accept. //amount would loop over the amount elements rather than the invoices, so every other invoice field would be lost.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Read XML

questions.scenario: You are loading a customer table and must update a customer's row if the key already exists, or insert a new row if it does not.
questions.prompt: Which step does both, based on the key?
options: Combination lookup/update
Insert / update
Table output
Update
questions.explanation: Insert / update looks each row up by its key, updates the row if it finds one and inserts it if not. Table output only inserts, so an existing key causes a duplicate or a failure. Update only updates existing rows and skips or fails on new ones. Combination lookup/update maintains junk dimensions with surrogate keys, not ordinary upserts.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Table Insert/Update

questions.scenario: Finance asks which region a customer was in on 1 March, even though the customer has since moved. The customer dimension is maintained as a Type 2 slowly changing dimension.
questions.prompt: Why can the dimension answer that?
options: It keeps a row per version, each with valid dates
It keeps only the changes since the last load
It keeps a version flag per row, but no dates
It keeps the latest value, overwritten in place
questions.explanation: Type 2 adds a row for each change, with valid-from and valid-to dates, so a point-in-time question finds the version that was current on 1 March. Overwriting in place is Type 1, which could not answer it. A version flag without dates cannot place a version in time. Keeping only the latest changes would lose the older history the question needs.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Slowly Changing Dimensions

questions.scenario: A developer needs to read and write objects in a MinIO bucket running on-premises.
questions.prompt: How do you connect PDI to that bucket?
options: Create an S3-compatible VFS connection to MinIO
Use an HDFS path in the Hadoop file input step
Create a JDBC connection to the MinIO server
Install a dedicated MinIO plugin from Marketplace
questions.explanation: MinIO speaks the S3 protocol, so an S3-compatible VFS connection pointed at its endpoint reads and writes it exactly as it would AWS S3. JDBC is for databases, not object storage. HDFS is Hadoop's file system, a different protocol. No dedicated plugin is needed, because S3 support is built in.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — MinIO

questions.scenario: The first step of a new transformation must take the rows returned by a SELECT that joins two tables in a PostgreSQL source.
questions.prompt: Which step runs that query and passes its rows downstream?
options: Database lookup
Database join
Execute SQL script
Table input
questions.explanation: Table input runs a SELECT against a connection and emits each result row, so it starts a stream. Database lookup fetches values for rows already in a stream. Execute SQL script runs statements but does not produce their result rows as a stream. Database join runs a query for each incoming row, so it needs an input stream first.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Reading from a Database

questions.scenario: A monthly transformation writes to an Excel workbook, and each run must add its rows below the previous month's rather than replacing the file.
questions.prompt: How do you configure the Microsoft Excel writer step?
options: Reuse the file and sheet, starting at the sheet's end
Replace the output file on every run
Use Text file output with an .xlsx extension
Write a new workbook with the date in its name
questions.explanation: Excel writer can reuse the existing file and sheet and start writing at the end of the sheet, appending below last month's rows. Replacing the file on each run loses the earlier months. A new dated workbook each month keeps the data but not in one sheet. Text file output writes plain text, so an .xlsx name would not make it a workbook.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Excel Writer

questions.scenario: A nightly export produces millions of rows, and the team wants each output file capped at a manageable number of rows.
questions.prompt: Which Text file output setting does that?
options: Buffer size, set to the file size wanted
Add date to filename, for a file per run
Limit, set to the maximum rows to write
Split every ... rows, set to the row limit
questions.explanation: Split every ... rows starts a new output file after that many rows, so each file stays capped. Limit is a Text file input setting that stops reading; it would drop rows rather than split them. Buffer size affects reading performance, not the size of output files. Adding the date to the filename gives one file per run, each still holding every row.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Text File Output

questions.scenario: A developer sets up a new connection to a MySQL database, but Spoon reports that the driver cannot be found.
questions.prompt: What must be added for PDI to connect?
options: An ODBC data source for the MySQL server
The MySQL JDBC driver JAR, in data-integration/lib
The MySQL command-line client, on the PATH
A MySQL connector plugin from Marketplace
questions.explanation: PDI connects to databases over JDBC, and the MySQL driver is not bundled, so its JAR goes in data-integration/lib and Spoon is restarted. The command-line client is not used by PDI. An ODBC data source is not the route PDI's MySQL connection takes. No plugin is needed; the driver JAR is the missing piece.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Connecting to a Database

questions.scenario: You join an orders stream to a customers stream with Merge join on customer_id. The orders come from a Table input with no ORDER BY, and the customers from a CSV in file order.
questions.prompt: What must be true of both inputs before the join?
options: Both have unique customer_id values
Both come from the same database connection
Both are sorted on customer_id, in the same direction
Both have the same number of rows
questions.explanation: Merge join walks the two streams in step, so both must be sorted on the join key in the same direction; add ORDER BY to the query and a Sort rows after the CSV. The streams can have any number of rows each. They can come from any sources. Keys need not be unique; a key can match several rows.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Merge Join

questions.scenario: A fact table carries four low-cardinality flags: payment type, channel, promotion and gift wrap. The warehouse design folds them into one junk dimension with a surrogate key per combination.
questions.prompt: Which step maintains that dimension?
options: Dimension lookup/update
Combination lookup/update
Database lookup
Insert / update
questions.explanation: Combination lookup/update assigns a surrogate key to each new combination of its input fields and reuses it when the combination appears again, which is exactly a junk dimension. Dimension lookup/update maintains slowly changing dimensions keyed on a natural key. Insert / update upserts rows by key but does not issue surrogate keys for combinations. Database lookup only reads.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Slowly Changing Dimensions

questions.scenario: A CSV you are reading has text fields wrapped in double quotes because they contain commas.
questions.prompt: Which Text file input setting reads those fields correctly?
options: Separator, set to a character never used
Enclosure, set to the double quote
Escape, set to the comma
Lazy conversion, turned off
questions.explanation: Enclosure tells the step which character wraps a field, so commas inside the quotes are kept as data rather than treated as separators. Escape marks a single character to take literally; setting it to the comma would corrupt the separators. Changing the separator breaks every ordinary row of the file. Lazy conversion affects when types are converted, not how fields are split.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Data Sources — Text File Input

questions.scenario: You must enrich five million order rows with customer data from a two-million-row database table. A colleague suggests Database join; you are weighing it against Merge join.
questions.prompt: Which statements correctly contrast the two steps?
options: Merge join needs both inputs sorted on the join key
Database join is faster than Merge join at this size
Database join needs its input sorted on the join key
Merge join runs a SQL query for each incoming row
Database join runs a SQL query for each incoming row
questions.explanation: Database join runs a SQL query for each incoming row, which is flexible but means five million queries here. Merge join needs both inputs sorted on the join key and then walks them together. Database join is not faster at this size; per-row queries are the slow part. Merge join issues no per-row SQL. Database join needs no sorted input.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enriching the Dataset — Database Join

questions.scenario: A transformation that should output about 5,000 rows produces several million, and the run never finishes.
questions.prompt: Which step most likely explains that?
options: Merge join, duplicating rows from an unsorted input
Stream lookup, returning every row that matches a key
Join rows, emitting every combination of its two inputs
Database join, re-querying and multiplying each row
questions.explanation: Join rows is the Cartesian product: 2,000 rows against 2,500 is five million, usually because it was used where a keyed join was meant. Merge join on unsorted input misses matches rather than multiplying rows. Database join returns what its query returns for each row; it does not multiply the stream on its own. Stream lookup returns at most one match per row.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enriching the Dataset — Join Rows

questions.scenario: A transformation runs millions of rows through a Database lookup against a small, static reference table, and the developer wants to cut the repeated round-trips to the database.
questions.prompt: What does enabling the lookup cache avoid?
options: Schema validation errors on the lookup table
Repeating a query for a key it has already seen
Running out of connections in the pool
Race conditions between concurrent step copies
questions.explanation: With the cache on, each looked-up result is kept in memory, so a key already seen is answered without another query. It does nothing about race conditions between step copies. It does not manage connections in a pool. Schema validation is not something a lookup performs.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enriching the Dataset — Database Lookups

questions.scenario: You compare yesterday's customer extract, the reference stream, with today's, the compare stream, using Merge rows (diff). Customer 1042 is in yesterday's extract but missing from today's.
questions.prompt: Which flag does Merge rows (diff) give that customer?
options: removed
changed
new
deleted
questions.explanation: A row present in the reference stream and absent from the compare stream is flagged deleted. new is for a row that appears only in the compare stream. changed is for a row in both whose values differ. removed is not one of the step's flags, which are new, changed, deleted and identical.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enriching the Dataset — Merge Rows (diff)

questions.scenario: An analyst hands you pricing rules written as spreadsheet formulas, such as IF([qty] > 100; [bulk_price]; [list_price]), and wants them carried into a transformation as written.
questions.prompt: Which step evaluates those expressions most directly?
options: User defined Java class
Formula
Calculator
Modified JavaScript value
questions.explanation: Formula evaluates spreadsheet-style expressions such as IF, with fields referenced in square brackets, so the rules carry over almost unchanged. Calculator offers a fixed list of operations and cannot express a conditional formula. Modified JavaScript value could do it, but each rule would have to be rewritten as JavaScript. User defined Java class would need them rewritten as Java code.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enriching the Dataset — Formula

questions.scenario: An e-commerce company receives a high-volume stream of order data, and each order includes a two-letter country code. The company needs to enrich each order with the full country name from a static list of valid country codes.
questions.prompt: Which characteristic makes Stream lookup the most efficient method for this enrichment?
options: The reference data set is small enough to be fully cached in memory, enabling very fast lookups.
Stream lookup automatically handles updates to the reference data set without requiring a restart.
Stream lookup is optimized to handle large reference data sets that exceed available memory.
Stream lookup can return multiple matching country names for a single country code.
questions.explanation: 'The reference data set is small enough to be fully cached in memory, enabling very fast lookups' — Correct: Stream lookup excels when the entire reference set can be held in memory, providing rapid access. 'Stream lookup automatically handles updates to the reference data set without requiring a restart' — Incorrect: Stream lookup requires a restart if the reference data changes. 'Stream lookup is optimized to handle large reference data sets that exceed available memory' — Incorrect: Stream lookup performance degrades significantly with large reference data sets that do not fit in memory. 'Stream lookup can return multiple matching country names for a single country code' — Incorrect: Stream lookup typically returns a single match per input row.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enriching the Dataset — Lookups

questions.scenario: A Group by step totals sales per region, but the output lists the North region several times, each with a partial total.
questions.prompt: What is missing upstream of the Group by?
options: A Sort rows step on the region field
A limit on the number of input rows
A Select values step aligning the types
An aggregation that pre-sums each region
questions.explanation: Group by totals consecutive rows with the same key, so an unsorted input splits one region into several groups; sorting on region first fixes it, or Memory group by avoids the need. Pre-summing would do the step's job for it and still needs grouping. Limiting the rows would hide the problem, not fix it. Field types are not what splits the groups.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enriching the Dataset

questions.scenario: A new rule sets a discount from several conditions together: the customer's tier, the order size, and whether the order date falls in a promotion window.
questions.prompt: Why does this rule call for Modified JavaScript value rather than Calculator?
options: Calculator works on batches, not single rows
It runs faster than Calculator on every row
Calculator can only handle numeric fields
It can express arbitrary per-row logic with conditions
questions.explanation: Modified JavaScript value runs full per-row logic, so nested conditions across several fields are straightforward. It is slower than Calculator, not faster. Calculator handles dates and strings as well as numbers, but only through its fixed list of operations. Calculator works row by row, like every step.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enriching the Dataset — Modified JavaScript Value

questions.scenario: You need to remove duplicate rows from a stream based on a single key field, and the stream arrives in no particular order.
questions.prompt: Which steps remove the duplicates correctly?
options: Select values with the key marked unique
Stream lookup of the stream against itself
Unique rows on its own, keyed on the field
Sort rows on the key, then Unique rows
questions.explanation: Unique rows compares each row only with the one before it, so sorting on the key first brings duplicates together; Unique rows (HashSet) is the variant that avoids sorting at the cost of memory. On its own, Unique rows misses duplicates that are not adjacent. A Stream lookup against itself enriches rows rather than removing them. Select values has no uniqueness setting.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enriching the Dataset

questions.scenario: A Filter rows step checks qty > 0. You connect one step for orders with a quantity and another for orders without.
questions.prompt: How does Filter rows route the orders?
options: All rows continue, each flagged true or false
True rows to one step, false rows to the other
Matching rows continue; the rest are dropped
Non-matching rows continue; the rest are dropped
questions.explanation: Filter rows has a true hop and a false hop, and with both connected each order goes to exactly one of the two steps. Dropping the rest only happens to a hop left unconnected, which is not the case here. Non-matching rows do not replace matching ones. The step routes rows; it does not add a flag field and pass everything on.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enriching the Dataset

questions.scenario: A data integration specialist is building a Pentaho Data Integration (PDI) transformation to calculate a discount based on customer loyalty status. The discount amount must be dynamically calculated for each customer record as part of a larger data flow.
questions.prompt: Within a PDI transformation, what is the primary function of the Formula step?
options: The Formula step establishes connections to relational databases for direct data retrieval.
The Formula step provides a mechanism for generating synthetic data to validate transformation logic.
The Formula step automatically categorizes and tags fields based on their data type.
The Formula step evaluates Formula Expressions to derive new field values.
questions.explanation: 'The Formula step evaluates Formula Expressions to derive new field values' — Correct: This accurately describes the core purpose of the Formula step – performing calculations and creating derived data. 'The Formula step provides a mechanism for generating synthetic data to validate transformation logic' — Incorrect: The ‘Generate rows’ step is responsible for generating test data, and the Formula step operates on the data provided to it. 'The Formula step automatically categorizes and tags fields based on their data type' — Incorrect: Data categorization and tagging are not functions of the Formula step. 'The Formula step establishes connections to relational databases for direct data retrieval' — Incorrect: Database connections are handled by dedicated input steps, such as ‘Table Input’.
questions.source: Formula

questions.scenario: A data analyst needs to enrich a dataset with information from a database based on values within each row of the incoming data.
questions.prompt: What is a key characteristic of the Database Join step in Pentaho Data Integration?
options: Every result row the database returned was appended to a copy of the input row.
The Database Join step automatically classifies data for easier search and retrieval.
The Database Join step is most efficient when processing millions of rows of data.
The Database Join step merges tables within the database using standard join operations.
questions.explanation: 'Every result row the database returned was appended to a copy of the input row.' — Correct: This accurately describes how the Database Join step handles output, adding database results to each input row. 'The Database Join step merges tables within the database using standard join operations.' — Incorrect: The Database Join step does *not* perform a traditional database join; it executes queries for each input row. 'The Database Join step automatically classifies data for easier search and retrieval.' — Incorrect: Data classification is not a function of the Database Join step. 'The Database Join step is most efficient when processing millions of rows of data.' — Incorrect: The Database Join step is explicitly stated to be inefficient at large scales because it makes a round trip to the database for each row.
questions.source: Database Join

questions.scenario: A nightly process must download a file, load it with two transformations in order, and email the team if either load fails.
questions.prompt: Why is this built as a job rather than a transformation?
options: A job processes the file's rows faster
A transformation cannot accept parameters
A transformation cannot read downloaded files
A job sequences entries and branches on the outcome
questions.explanation: A job orchestrates: it runs entries in order, such as a download, two transformations and a mail, and follows success or failure hops. Jobs do not process rows at all, so they are not faster at it. Transformations accept parameters. A transformation can read any file present when it runs.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enterprise Solution — Hello World Job

questions.scenario: In a job, a developer wants a follow-on entry to run only when the preceding entry completes successfully.
questions.prompt: Which kind of hop should connect the two entries?
options: A hop followed only on a false result
An unconditional hop
A hop from an entry set to run in parallel
A hop followed only when the result is true
questions.explanation: A hop evaluated on a true result, shown green, runs the next entry only when the previous one succeeded. An unconditional hop runs the next entry whatever happened. A hop on a false result runs it only after a failure. Running next entries in parallel is an entry setting about launching entries together, not a condition on success.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enterprise Solution — Order of Execution

questions.scenario: A data pipeline uses a transformation that expects an input folder location. This location is defined by a parameter named IN_DIR. The transformation is executed both by a nightly batch job and interactively from the command line using Pan, often with different folder paths each time.
questions.prompt: How does the transformation resolve the correct input folder location for each execution?
options: The transformation uses the value of the IN_DIR parameter, which is set by the calling process at runtime.
The transformation reads the input folder path from the first row of data in the input stream.
The transformation retrieves the input folder path from a pre-configured value within the .ktr file.
The transformation obtains the input folder path from the kettle.properties file on the server hosting the transformation.
questions.explanation: 'The transformation uses the value of the IN_DIR parameter, which is set by the calling process at runtime.' — Correct: Parameters allow external control of transformation behavior, and their values are supplied when the transformation runs. 'The transformation reads the input folder path from the first row of data in the input stream.' — Incorrect: This describes a method of passing data, not configuration parameters. Parameters and input data are distinct concepts. 'The transformation retrieves the input folder path from a pre-configured value within the .ktr file.' — Incorrect: The .ktr file stores the parameter *definition*, but not the runtime value, which is overridden by the calling process. 'The transformation obtains the input folder path from the kettle.properties file on the server hosting the transformation.' — Incorrect: kettle.properties stores system-wide properties, not per-transformation or per-execution parameters.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enterprise Solution — Parameters

questions.scenario: You are creating a run configuration in Spoon for a transformation that must run on a remote Carte server rather than on your laptop.
questions.prompt: What should the run configuration target?
options: The repository, which forwards the run to Carte
Pentaho local, with the Carte host in a variable
An embedded JVM container on the remote host
The Pentaho engine, running on the Carte server
questions.explanation: A run configuration targets the Pentaho engine either locally or on a remote Carte server, so choosing the Carte server sends the run there. Pentaho local always runs inside Spoon on your machine, whatever a variable holds. There is no embedded-JVM-container target. A repository stores transformations; it does not execute or forward them.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enterprise Solution — Run Configurations

questions.scenario: A scheduler on a Linux server with no Spoon installed must run a nightly job (.kjb) and, separately, a standalone transformation (.ktr).
questions.prompt: Which command-line APIs run them?
options: spoon.sh in headless mode, for both of them
Pan for the job, and Kitchen for the transformation
Kitchen for the job, and Pan for the transformation
Carte for both, started once as a service
questions.explanation: Kitchen runs jobs and Pan runs transformations, each to completion from the command line, which suits a scheduler. The reverse pairing is wrong in both directions. Carte is a long-running server that accepts runs over HTTP, not a scheduler's one-shot tool. Spoon is the designer and has no headless mode for running files.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enterprise Solution — Run Configurations

questions.scenario: A transformation declares a parameter named REGION. It is sometimes run with no value supplied, and must then use EMEA.
questions.prompt: Where is that default value set?
options: In a Set variables step at the transformation's start
On the Parameters tab of each calling job
On the Parameters tab of the transformation's settings
In kettle.properties on the host that runs it
questions.explanation: The transformation's own Parameters tab declares REGION and gives it the default EMEA, used whenever no caller supplies a value. kettle.properties sets machine-wide variables, not a parameter's declared default. A calling job can override the value, but that is the caller's value, not the default. A Set variables step cannot give its own transformation a parameter default.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enterprise Solution — Parameters

questions.scenario: The operations team wants an email automatically each time the nightly load job finishes.
questions.prompt: Which job entry sends that email?
options: HTTP
Mail validator
Mail
Write to log
questions.explanation: The Mail entry sends an SMTP message and is usually placed on the success or failure hop of the entry that matters. Mail validator checks that an address is valid; it sends nothing. Write to log writes to the execution log, which nobody receives by email. HTTP calls a web address; it is not an email sender.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enterprise Solution — Jobs

questions.scenario: An administrator adds DB_HOST to kettle.properties on the server. A job and the three transformations it calls all reference ${DB_HOST}.
questions.prompt: Where is DB_HOST available when the job runs?
options: In the three transformations, but not the job
In the job and in all three transformations
Only after a Set variables step has run
Only on the master node in a clustered run
questions.explanation: Variables in kettle.properties are loaded when PDI starts and are available to every job and transformation in that process - global scope. Jobs see them as well as transformations. No Set variables step is needed; that is for setting variables during a run. They are loaded on every node that runs PDI, not only a master.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enterprise Solution — Parameters and Variables

questions.scenario: Four developers will work on the same transformations, and the team already runs all code review through Git.
questions.prompt: Which repository choice fits this team best?
options: File-based, giving up the database's locking and shared security
Either one, since the choice has no effect on collaboration
File-based, the only option that works without a server
Database-backed, the only option for several developers
questions.explanation: A file-based repository is a folder of .ktr and .kjb files, so the team's existing branching, review and history apply to pipelines too; what it gives up is the database repository's record locking, shared connections and central permissions. Several developers can use either kind, so a database is not the only option. File-based is not the only serverless choice. The choice shapes collaboration directly, which is the point of the question.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enterprise Solution

questions.scenario: Operations want one tool that runs a nightly job from cron and exits, and another that stays running so remote transformations can be sent to it over HTTP.
questions.prompt: Which Pentaho services can be used for each role?
options: Kitchen runs the job and exits; Carte stays up for HTTP
Pan runs the job and exits; Kitchen stays up for HTTP
Kitchen fills both roles, started with a service flag
Carte runs the job and exits; Kitchen stays up for HTTP
questions.explanation: Kitchen runs a job to completion and exits, which suits cron, while Carte is a long-running HTTP server that accepts runs, used for remote and clustered execution. The reverse pairing swaps their natures. Kitchen has no server mode. Pan runs transformations, not jobs, and Kitchen is never a server.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enterprise Solution — Run Configurations

questions.scenario: A clustered transformation runs across one Carte master and two slave servers, with its heavy aggregation steps marked as clustered.
questions.prompt: What does the master do during the run?
options: Only stores the logs that the slaves write
Distributes rows to the slaves and gathers their results
Processes every row itself while the slaves wait
Holds the database connection pool for the slaves
questions.explanation: The master coordinates: it sends rows to the slaves, which do the heavy work in parallel, and collects their results into one stream. Processing every row itself would make the cluster pointless. It does not act as a connection pool for the slaves. Logging is not its only role.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - Practitioner: Enterprise Solution — Run Configurations

questions.scenario: A data integration developer is setting up a new workstation and wants to ensure the Pentaho Data Integration (PDI) environment is optimized for rapid development, especially given a database schema that changes frequently.
questions.prompt: Which option, when disabled in Spoon’s ‘General’ settings, would be most beneficial in this scenario?
options: Show tips at startup?
Use database cache
Ask user when exiting?
Show repository dialog at startup?
questions.explanation: 'Use database cache' — Correct: Disabling this ensures Spoon always reflects the latest database schema, which is critical when the schema is frequently altered. 'Show tips at startup?' — Incorrect: This is a user interface setting and doesn't impact data integration accuracy or performance related to schema changes. 'Show repository dialog at startup?' — Incorrect: This affects repository connections, not local schema handling. 'Ask user when exiting?' — Incorrect: This is a convenience feature and unrelated to schema synchronization.
questions.source: Configuring PDI
